explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The text says Milcah is the daughter of Haran, who was the father of both Milcah and Iscah. That's the same Haran who died in Ur, and he was Nahor's brother. So Nahor's wife comes from his own brother's household. Genesis keeps its family records tight.

Close, but the text says otherwise. Milcah, Nahor's wife, is the daughter of Haran, who was the father of both Milcah and Iscah. Iscah is one more name to tuck in your apron pocket. And Haran is the brother who died in Ur, so the answer is a plain True.

That's it, friend. The text says, “But Sarai was barren; she had no children.” Notice how short that is after all those long lists of sons and daughters. It reads like the writer set down his pen and let the quiet sit there. I think that quiet is the whole point.

I get it, since the lists before this are full of sons. But the text says Sarai was barren and had no children. Not many sons, and not one. After a whole stretch of fathers and sons, her line stands out as the empty one.

That's a fair guess after all those lines about sons and daughters. But the text says, “But Sarai was barren; she had no children.” No children means no daughter either. The writer has been giving fathers and their sons and daughters, then stops on her with one short sentence, and it stands out.

I see why that sounds believable, since Lot's father Haran has died. But the text says Terah took “…his grandson Lot son of Haran…” along with Abram and Sarai. Lot is part of the group that sets out from Ur of the Chaldeans. He gets a spot in the lineup.

That's right, baker. The text says Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot son of Haran, and his daughter-in-law Sarai. So Lot goes with them when they set out from Ur. His father Haran died back in Ur, and Lot is still part of the family caravan.

That's right! The text says that when they arrived in Haran, they settled there. It's the same name as Terah's son Haran, who died in Ur, so keep them straight: one is a man and one is a place. They set out for Canaan, and this is where they stop instead.

Babel is where the LORD confused the language of the whole world (Genesis 11:9). It comes up just before this passage, but it isn't where this family settles. The text says they settle in Haran. Same book, different stop on the map, friend.

Nineveh is the great city God sends Jonah to (Jonah 1:2). It never comes up in this passage. The text says that when Terah's family arrives in Haran, they settle there. Nineveh belongs to a different story.

Yes, friend. Terah lives 205 years, and he dies in Haran. The family set out for Canaan, but Terah's story ends there in Haran. The writer doesn't dress it up, and neither will I. Sometimes the plain truth is the whole lesson.

Not quite. The text says Terah lived 205 years, and he died in Haran (Genesis 11:32). Ur is where the family set out from, but the text says nothing about him going back there. I think this one is a heavy line, and the writer states it plainly.

That's an ambitious guess, but the text doesn't say that. It says Terah lived 205 years, and he died in Haran. No city and no building project, just the end of his life. Terah's part of the story closes right there.

explanations.answer: To a land God will show him
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker! God says, “…go to the land I will show you.” In His words to Abram, the place isn't named, only the promise that He will show him. That takes real trust, friend. I'd have asked for directions twice and then packed extra cookie boxes.

explanations.answer: East to the land of Shinar
explanations.explanation: Shinar is where people settled earlier in Genesis (Genesis 11:2), but God doesn't send Abram there. He says, “…go to the land I will show you.” No name is given yet. Abram has to follow the LORD one step at a time.

explanations.answer: Down to the land of Egypt
explanations.explanation: God doesn't mention Egypt when He speaks to Abram. He says, “…go to the land I will show you.” The place hasn't even been named yet. That's what makes the call such a big one.

That's it, friend! God says, “I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you…” A nation is a whole lot of people. That's like holding one lonely cookie and being told it will fill a stadium. Now that's a promise with some size to it.
A king would be a big title, but that's not what God says. The promise is, “I will make you into a great nation…” A nation is a whole lot of people. That's even bigger than one throne.

That one sounds fancy, but God doesn't say it. He says, “I will make you into a great nation…” So the promise is about a whole people coming from Abram. A prince would be a pretty small cookie next to that.

Yes, baker. God says, “I will make your name great, so that you will be a blessing.” Notice the “so that.” The name is tied to being a blessing. That's how God puts it, and the very next thing He says is that all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abram.
Not quite. God does promise this, in His own words: “I will make your name great, so that you will be a blessing.” It's right there in the middle of His promises to Abram. So this one is True.

explanations.answer: To all the families of the earth
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend! God says, “…all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” That's not just one neighborhood. It's every family on earth. For an old man who hasn't even found the land yet, that's a promise bigger than the whole map.

That's a good-sized guess, but God goes bigger. He says, “…all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” Canaan is where Abram is headed, but the promise doesn't stop at its borders. It reaches all the families of the earth.

I see why you'd pick it, since Abram is the one the blessing comes through. But God says, “…all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” That's a much bigger circle than one household. It reaches every family on earth.

That's right, baker. The text says, “So Abram departed, as the LORD had directed him…” He has the promises but not the address, and he goes anyway. The text also tells us he was seventy-five years old when he left Haran.

I see why you'd wonder, with no land named yet. But the text says, “So Abram departed, as the LORD had directed him…” He goes, and Lot goes with him. It also says Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran.

Yes, friend! The text says Abram took his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, and all their possessions and people, and set out for the land of Canaan. Then it says, “When they came to the land of Canaan…” Terah's trip stopped in Haran, but this one gets all the way there.

Terah's trip did stop in Haran, so I understand the worry. But Abram's trip goes farther. The text says they set out for the land of Canaan, and then, “When they came to the land of Canaan…” So this time the family arrives.

It would make sense for a promised land to be empty, but the text says otherwise. It says, “And at that time the Canaanites were in the land.” People already live there. So Abram arrives as a traveler passing through someone else's neighborhood.

You got it, baker! Abram travels through the land as far as the Oak of Moreh at Shechem (Genesis 12:6). Then the text says, “And at that time the Canaanites were in the land.” So the land has people in it already. Abram shows up as the new face in town, and I bet he didn't know where the good parking was.

That's right, friend! The LORD says, “I will give this land to your offspring.” Offspring means Abram's descendants, the family that's still to come. Think about it. Sarai has no children yet, and God is already talking about a whole inheritance.

Lot, Abram's nephew, is traveling right alongside him, so I get the guess. But the LORD says, “I will give this land to your offspring.” That's Abram's own descendants. Lot isn't named in the promise.
Nahor is Abram's brother, so it's a natural guess. But the LORD doesn't name him. He says, “I will give this land to your offspring.” The promise is about Abram's own offspring.
Yes, baker. The text says, “So Abram built an altar there to the LORD, who had appeared to him.” He builds it right where the LORD appeared. The promise was spoken, and an altar went up.

A tower makes me think of Babel, where the people said they would build a city with a tower (Genesis 11:4). But that isn't what Abram builds here. The text says, “So Abram built an altar there to the LORD, who had appeared to him.” An altar, friend.

A city is a big project, but the text doesn't say Abram builds one. It says, “So Abram built an altar there to the LORD, who had appeared to him.” What goes up is an altar, built to the LORD. That's the only thing the text says he builds there.

That's right, friend! The text says Abram moved on to the hill country east of Bethel and pitched his tent. Then, “There he built an altar to the LORD, and he called on the name of the LORD.” That makes a second altar in the land, after the one where the LORD appeared to him.

I can see why you'd doubt it, but the text says it plainly. Abram pitches his tent, and then, “There he built an altar to the LORD, and he called on the name of the LORD.” That makes a second altar in the land. So this one is True.
